title: Installing or Moving a Gas Fireplace in Marpole: Plan the Gas Line Before the Wall
description: Plan a Marpole gas fireplace installation or relocation: service scope, a Valor H5 input example, a measured gas-line route, shared loads and approvals.
imageAlt: Valor H5 1100M fireplace in the manufacturer’s photographed room setting, with a Gasfitter.ca brand label
imageCredit: Valor Fireplaces / Miles Industries official H5 product photograph. Manufacturer setting, not a Marpole customer installation or work by Gasfitter.ca.
contentOrigin: Original sourced service-planning guide; hypothetical route and shared-load examples, not a surveyed property.
intro: Installing a gas fireplace or moving one to another wall in Marpole starts with an installation assessment, not a choice of trim. Ask a licensed gas contractor to review the gas-line route, actual connected loads, proposed appliance and complete installation scope before you close walls or order finishes. A nearby gas pipe does not establish that a new fireplace can be connected, and moving an existing unit is not simply a furniture move.

This guide is about preparing a gas-line and fireplace installation enquiry. It uses the natural-gas Valor H5 1100MN as a specific documentation example, not a recommendation for your home or an offer to supply that appliance. The measured route and other appliance inputs below are fictional teaching examples. Use the Gasfitter.ca sketch planner to organize the facts for qualified review; it does not approve pipe sizing, pressure loss, meter capacity or installation feasibility.

sections.heading: Decide whether you need installation, relocation or repair
paragraphs: An installation enquiry should describe what you want changed. Is this a new fireplace where none exists, a replacement in the same location, or a proposal to relocate an existing appliance? Explain what will happen to the original unit and connection. If your actual problem is a fireplace that will not operate, start with a repair assessment instead of assuming replacement or relocation is necessary. A symptom and a proposed renovation are different briefs, even when they concern the same fireplace.

For a repair enquiry, record what you observed, when the problem occurs and any displayed message, without opening the appliance or attempting gas adjustments. Provide the existing model and service records if safely available. For an installation enquiry, provide the proposed location and the stage of the renovation. Tell the contractor which decision you need first: whether the project merits a site assessment, what information is missing, or what scope a written quotation should cover. Do not turn an online planning article into a diagnosis of a particular fault.

sections.heading: Make the Marpole address useful without guessing the building
paragraphs: The City describes Marpole as an area with a mix of residential housing, including low-rise apartments, and commercial streets. That is useful local context, but it does not identify the gas arrangement, construction, ownership or alteration permissions at your address. A detached-home enquiry and an apartment enquiry can require different information. State the actual property type and your authority to request work, rather than relying on a neighbourhood label to imply that every building has the same installation options.

Provide the project address privately to the contractor, together with legitimate access arrangements. If the fireplace would affect a shared wall, exterior surface or common space, identify that question early and obtain the relevant property approval process. Do not assume permission to use a shared area just because it is physically accessible. A site visit should be arranged through the person responsible for access; this guide establishes no local office, completed Marpole project, booking availability or right to carry out work.

sections.heading: Use an exact appliance record, not the family name alone
paragraphs: The current Valor H5 installation manual identifies 1100MN as natural gas and 1100MP as propane. For the natural-gas example, its maximum input is 30,000 BTU/h and minimum input is 16,000 BTU/h. Use the exact model and verified fuel configuration when preparing the proposed-load record. The H5 family name by itself is not a complete identification for an older appliance. Keep the rating information and matching document revision with the brief for the contractor to confirm.

For the worked planning example, enter the documented maximum input of 30,000 BTU/h for the proposed 1100MN, subject to verification against the actual appliance. Do not substitute a heat-output figure or the lower operating input because it makes a subtotal smaller. If the supplied model, fuel or rating is different, correct the record before comparing proposals. Where the information has not been confirmed, leave the input unknown and label the missing evidence instead of copying a number from a similar-looking fireplace.

sections.heading: A gas-line quotation needs a complete work boundary
paragraphs: Ask a proposal to separate the gas-line assessment from appliance supply, removal, venting work, wall preparation and finishing. Explain whether you already own the fireplace or are still choosing one. A gas-line quotation should not silently become a promise to provide every part of a fireplace installation. Equally, an appliance price should not be mistaken for a complete installed project. Name the people responsible for the parts of the job that must fit together.

Consider an owner who wants the fireplace moved from one wall to another during a living-room renovation. A useful brief says what will be removed, what is proposed, which finishes remain open and who is coordinating the trades. It also asks what must be assessed before framing dimensions are finalized. This is a hypothetical coordination example, not evidence that relocation is possible in a particular home. The contractor may identify missing records, a different scope or a reason to reconsider the proposed position.

sections.heading: Keep the gas route separate from the venting question
paragraphs: Draw the proposed gas connection and the proposed fireplace location as distinct information. A line on the gas sketch does not describe an approved vent path. Do not infer a suitable termination from an attractive exterior wall or an existing opening. Provide photographs of the relevant areas only where you can take them safely and legitimately, and ask the installer what site observations are needed. Label concealed or unverified areas rather than completing the drawing from imagination.

The matching Valor installation manual covers framing, clearances and approved venting as well as the gas supply. Those are installer requirements, not dimensions to infer from the featured photograph. Ask the installer to confirm the complete arrangement and required documents for the actual appliance and location. Keep cabinetry, wall finishes, furniture placement and any planned equipment above the fireplace on the coordination list. Do not use a generic diagram or this article to authorize cutting a wall, altering a vent or connecting gas.

sections.heading: Worked route: a 42-foot entered path, not a pipe-size answer
paragraphs: For a fictional sketch, suppose the documented meter-to-junction section is 16 feet. A proposed fireplace branch then has 22 measured feet of horizontal routing and a separate 4-foot rise that was not included in that measurement. The entered fireplace path is 16 + 22 + 4 = 42 feet. An existing furnace on a different branch is 11 feet beyond the same junction, making that entered path 16 + 11 = 27 feet. The longest complete entered path in this limited example is 42 feet.

The example teaches how to preserve the route relationship and avoid double counting. If a measurement already follows the rise, do not add the same vertical distance again. If a hidden section is unknown, the apparent total is incomplete. Record whether each section was measured, copied from reliable existing records or still requires confirmation. The 42-foot total does not establish a diameter, acceptable pressure drop, available meter capacity or an approved route. A professional must assess the actual system under the applicable requirements.

sections.heading: Shared-load example: separate replacement from addition
paragraphs: Use a separate fictional equipment list with an existing furnace input of 80,000 BTU/h and an existing water-heater input of 40,000 BTU/h, both assumed confirmed solely for this example. Adding the documented 30,000 BTU/h fireplace example produces a known entered subtotal of 150,000 BTU/h. The furnace and water-heater figures are teaching values, not ratings of equipment at a Marpole address. Replace them with the actual confirmed inputs when preparing a real brief.

A replacement needs a clear before-and-after list. If an old fireplace will be removed, identify it as removed rather than leaving both fireplaces counted as continuing equipment. If the old appliance will remain elsewhere, say so. Separate future ideas from equipment that is actually part of the proposal. An unknown input is not zero and should remain visible as an unknown alongside the known subtotal. The planner does not decide simultaneous use, allowable diversity or supply capacity; the contractor needs the actual connected arrangement and supporting records.

sections.heading: Build and check the sketch before sending the enquiry
paragraphs: Open the national gas-line planner and add the junction and appliances relevant to your brief. Give the proposed fireplace a recognizable label, choose its upstream connection and enter each known measured section. Add the separate rise only if it is additional. In the worked example, connect the fireplace and furnace to the same junction so the shared 16-foot section is represented once in the drawing and correctly included in each complete route. Review the resulting route and input totals before sharing anything.

Use the position controls to make symbols readable. Moving a symbol changes the presentation, not a measured pipe length or an installation decision. The planner can record pressure, meter and material details, sum entered lengths and known BTU/h, and preserve missing information. It does not calculate pressure loss, select pipe sizes or approve meter capacity. Save an editable plan if you expect revisions and export a readable brief for the contractor. Keep personal account details and information about other occupants out of a public sketch.

sections.heading: Pressure and meter details are evidence for assessment
paragraphs: A meter already serving a home does not establish spare capacity for a fireplace addition. Gather documented meter and pressure information where available and tell the contractor which details remain unknown. Do not operate a regulator, open a service enclosure or attempt a pressure test to fill in a form. A precise-looking number is useful only when its unit, source and meaning are known. The contractor needs to distinguish existing records from measurements taken during qualified assessment.

FortisBC provides a gas-service upgrade process where an upgrade is required. Ask the contractor whether utility involvement is necessary and who will provide the technical information. Do not assume either that an upgrade is inevitable or that an existing meter rules it out. Keep a utility request distinct from permission to install a fireplace. A submitted enquiry is not an installation approval, and an online subtotal cannot replace the supply review needed for the particular equipment, gas arrangement and property.

sections.heading: Confirm the permits for the actual scope
paragraphs: The City of Vancouver says new natural-gas installations and alterations require a gas permit, with jurisdiction depending on the actual installation. Technical Safety BC also explains that additions, replacements and removals are alterations requiring the appropriate permit before work. Ask the licensed contractor to identify the responsible authority and permit responsibility in the proposal. Do not treat a replacement or the removal of an old connection as automatically outside the permit process.

The City’s mechanical-permit guidance distinguishes changes from certain same-type, same-capacity replacements, and notes that a gas permit may still be required. Have the contractor confirm which mechanical, electrical, building or other approvals apply to this specific fireplace project. A relocation is not automatically the same scope as a like-for-like replacement. Ask for a written list of required approvals and the point at which work may proceed. Property consent, permit issuance and technical acceptance should remain separate records, not one vague “approved” note.

sections.heading: Compare installation proposals on the same assumptions
paragraphs: Send each contractor the same brief: existing equipment, proposed appliance, location, measured or unknown route sections, property constraints and the decisions still outstanding. Ask what the assessment can establish from documents and what requires a visit. A proposal should identify exclusions and how concealed conditions or changes will be handled. If the appliance selection changes, request an updated assessment rather than assuming that a similar cabinet means the gas and installation requirements are unchanged.

Clarify who arranges access, protects occupied areas, restores finishes and coordinates any interruption to other equipment. An assessment appointment is not a promise that installation can begin that day. Request the next decision and the information needed to reach it. This guide establishes no installed price, rebate, turnaround time, credential claim or booking. A useful comparison is between complete and clearly conditional scopes, with the same equipment and site assumptions, rather than between headline prices that describe different jobs.

sections.heading: Retain the assessed result and the final records
paragraphs: At completion, retain the actual appliance identification, relevant manuals, work record and applicable permit or declaration information supplied for the project. Ask the installer to explain the owner instructions and which future concerns require qualified service. If the final route, appliance or scope changed from the first enquiry, update your records and mark the earlier sketch as preliminary. The next person reviewing the system should be able to distinguish an owner’s initial proposal from the installed result.

The practical next step is a focused installation enquiry: “I am planning a gas fireplace at this location in Marpole. Here are the existing equipment records, proposed model and measured route sections; these other details remain unknown. Please confirm the assessment scope, installation responsibilities and approvals before finishes are committed.” That gives the contractor a usable starting point without claiming the project is feasible. For a fireplace that needs repair instead, send observations and service records and ask for diagnosis before deciding on replacement.

faqs.question: Can an existing gas fireplace simply be moved to another wall?
faqs.answer: Relocation requires assessment of the actual appliance, gas route, venting, property constraints and approvals. Do not assume an existing connection or opening establishes that the new location is suitable.

faqs.question: Which gas input is used for the Valor H5 example?
faqs.answer: The matching manual lists the natural-gas 1100MN at a maximum input of 30,000 BTU/h. Confirm the exact actual model, fuel and rating before using that value in a real equipment record.

faqs.question: Does the 42-foot route determine a pipe size?
faqs.answer: No. It only sums the fictional entered sections, 16 + 22 + 4 feet. Pressure loss, sizing, materials, connected loads and available supply require qualified assessment.

faqs.question: Does the planner approve the 150,000 BTU/h example?
faqs.answer: No. It sums the entered known inputs. The two existing appliance loads are hypothetical, and the subtotal does not approve meter capacity or installation feasibility.

faqs.question: Is the pictured fireplace a Marpole installation by Gasfitter.ca?
faqs.answer: No. The image is Valor’s official H5 manufacturer photograph, credited as a product setting. It is not a customer project, partnership or installation claim.

title: No Room on the Electrical Panel? Planning a Stove Gas Line in Fairview
description: Need a stove but have no room on the electrical panel? Plan a Fairview stove gas-line enquiry, electrical checks, strata permissions and shared gas loads.
imageAlt: Frigidaire Gallery GCFG3060BF in its official manufacturer kitchen photograph, with a small Gasfitter.ca label
imageCredit: Frigidaire / Electrolux official product photograph. Manufacturer promotional setting, not a Fairview property or a Gasfitter.ca installation.
contentOrigin: Original document-based consumer planning guide; no property assessment or completed installation claimed.
intro: Need a stove but have no room on your electrical panel? A gas line for a gas stove may be an option to investigate, but it is not an automatic solution to a full panel. The service discussed here is gas-line assessment and installation for your chosen stove, not selling or supplying ranges. A qualified electrician must first confirm what the panel constraint actually means and what electrical supply the exact gas appliance still needs.

For a Fairview strata, coordinate the proposed stove gas line with property permission, qualified gas-system assessment and the applicable permits. An existing gas appliance elsewhere in the building does not establish that your kitchen can be connected. This guide uses the Canadian Frigidaire Gallery GCFG3060BF only as a document-reading example. The worked route and other loads are hypothetical. The national Gasfitter.ca planner records technical inputs, measured routes and known loads; it does not approve pipe sizes, pressure loss, meter capacity or installation feasibility.

sections.heading: A full electrical panel: start with the actual constraint
paragraphs: No room for another breaker and insufficient electrical service capacity are different issues. Ask a qualified electrician to establish which concern applies, review the existing cooking circuit and identify the electrical requirements of the exact proposed stove. Do not assume a spare receptacle is a suitable appliance circuit, or that changing the cooking fuel removes every electrical requirement. Make that electrical assessment part of the project brief before ordering a stove or commissioning a new gas line.

For the GCFG3060BF example, the matching installation instructions specify a dedicated, grounded and polarized branch circuit protected at 15 amps, with the voltage confirmed from the serial plate. That is a model-specific requirement, not permission to reuse any existing outlet. Gas cooking still relies on electricity for functions described by the manufacturer. A qualified electrician needs to confirm the actual supply and any changes; this guide does not promise that you can avoid a panel upgrade.

The gas fitter's task is to assess and, where approved, provide the gas line serving the chosen stove. That involves the actual fuel, connected input, pressure arrangement, route, existing shared loads and required approvals. Keep the appliance purchase separate from that scope. A useful enquiry is: “I need a gas line for a stove because the electrical panel may constrain an electric option. Can you assess the gas route while my electrician confirms the appliance circuit?”

sections.heading: Why Fairview needs a property-specific enquiry
paragraphs: The City identifies Fairview as a Vancouver neighbourhood with its own history and area information. That establishes local context, not the construction or gas arrangement of an individual building. A neighbourhood name cannot tell a contractor whether your suite has a suitable branch, who owns a riser or how access to shared equipment is arranged. Give the actual property details privately when seeking an assessment, rather than treating an area guide as a survey of your building.

Frame the first question narrowly: “I am considering this exact natural-gas range in this location; what information and permissions are needed to assess it?” That is more useful than asking whether gas ranges are generally possible in Fairview. Explain whether you are replacing an existing gas range, changing from an electric appliance or moving the cooking position. These are different project briefs. Do not describe an electric-to-gas conversion as a straightforward replacement just because the proposed unit has the same nominal width.

sections.heading: Keep strata permission and technical approval separate
paragraphs: Read the current strata bylaws, rules and alteration process, and ask the strata manager or council which documents govern the proposal. BC’s strata-owner resource explains the importance of the actual strata bylaws and responsibilities. Do not assume the Standard Bylaws are the complete current rules for your property. Equally, do not treat a neighbour’s earlier renovation as permission for your own work. Ask for the applicable process and retain the written response with the project brief.

An administrative permission is not a gas-supply calculation, and a contractor’s technical opinion is not a substitute for any required property approval. Keep a short decision record with separate lines for the proposed work, the person authorized to approve access or alterations, and the professional responsible for the technical scope. If an answer is pending, label it pending. This avoids an email saying “approved” being interpreted more broadly than the person intended. No general article can determine ownership of a pipe or allocate legal responsibility for a specific strata.

sections.heading: Identify the Canadian model before comparing inputs
paragraphs: The Canadian Frigidaire specification sheet, version 09/26, explicitly includes GCFG3060BF. It lists cooktop burner figures of 18,000, 5,000, 14,000, 10,000 and 10,000 BTU, plus separate bake and broil entries of 18,000 and 13,500 BTU. These are component specifications. The document is planning information, not a verified complete connected-input entry for your actual appliance. Do not enter only the largest burner, or add every printed figure and declare that result the approved nameplate load.

Keep the complete model, intended fuel configuration and matching installation instructions together. Ask the contractor which complete appliance input belongs in the gas-system assessment and record its source. Where that value has not been confirmed, leave the planner input blank and explain why. A range with gas cooking also has electrical requirements; a gas specification does not establish the adequacy of an existing circuit. Have the relevant qualified professional identify that part of the scope. Do not use the manufacturer’s product photograph to infer connection locations, dimensions or clearances.

sections.heading: Build a useful equipment record without opening anything
paragraphs: Start with documents already in your possession: the current appliance model, installation paperwork, a previous service record and the proposed product documents. A safely accessible rating-label photograph may help the contractor identify equipment, but do not move a connected range, remove panels or enter a locked service space to obtain one. Say that a detail is inaccessible when that is the case. A truthful gap is much safer and more useful than a number copied from a similar-looking appliance online.

Separate existing equipment from proposed equipment. Record whether an appliance will remain, be removed or be replaced, so a quotation does not accidentally count both the old and new unit as continuing loads. Include known appliances sharing the relevant supply arrangement, while marking the boundary of your knowledge. You are not expected to inventory other residents’ private equipment. Ask the responsible building representative or contractor to establish any shared-system records needed for assessment. Keep serial photographs, account numbers and access arrangements in private correspondence rather than a public project description.

sections.heading: A worked longest measured route: 35 feet, with a clear boundary
paragraphs: Consider a fictional sketch in which a documented meter-to-junction section is 18 feet. From that junction, the proposed range branch has a 12-foot measured section and a 5-foot vertical part that has not already been included. The entered range route is 18+12+5=35 feet. Suppose a different existing appliance connects to the same junction through a 9-foot branch. That entered route is 18+9=27 feet. The longest complete route in this limited sketch is 35 feet, even though another appliance could have a larger input.

These figures demonstrate arithmetic, not a real Fairview installation or an acceptable route. Do not add the 5-foot rise again if the original 12-foot measurement already followed that vertical section. Do not replace an unknown concealed route with the straight-line distance between rooms. If the connection to the meter is unconfirmed, the drawing is incomplete and its apparent longest route is not a measured whole-system result. Write down which sections were measured, which came from existing documents and which still require verification. That distinction should travel with any exported brief.

sections.heading: Shared loads: show what the subtotal does and does not include
paragraphs: For a separate fictional load example, suppose two existing appliances have confirmed inputs of 60,000 and 40,000 BTU/h. Their known subtotal is 100,000 BTU/h. If the proposed range’s complete input is not yet confirmed, the honest record is 100,000 BTU/h of known existing input plus one proposed unknown. It is not a 100,000 BTU/h complete system, and the 18,000 BTU component figure from the range brochure must not silently fill the missing whole-appliance entry.

The shared 18-foot section in the route example serves both downstream branches. A contractor needs the actual connected arrangement, relevant loads and applicable professional sizing method. The longest distance and the largest appliance load answer different questions; neither by itself establishes a pipe diameter. The planner can reveal missing entries and preserve the relationship between branches. It does not determine diversity allowances, whether appliances operate together or how a regulator changes the assessment. Ask the professional to document the assumptions used, rather than choosing whichever online table produces the most convenient answer.

sections.heading: Use the planner as a record, not an approval engine
paragraphs: In the gas-line planner, add a junction and the appliances relevant to the sketch. For each item, choose the upstream connection and enter its measured section length. Enter additional vertical distance only where it is genuinely additional. Use the item label to distinguish an existing appliance from the proposed GCFG3060BF. The position controls move symbols for readability; moving a symbol does not measure a pipe, change a building or establish an approved installation route.

Record known pipe material and existing diameter only when you have a reliable basis. Leave unknowns explicitly unknown. Copy documented pressure information with its unit, and identify where it came from. The form provides pressure and meter fields so those records can accompany the enquiry; it does not calculate available capacity. Save an editable plan if you want to revise it later and export a readable brief for the contractor. Review that export before sending it. The tool does not automatically send an enquiry, and your drawing should not contain private information about neighbours.

sections.heading: Ask who controls access and a possible service interruption
paragraphs: A useful strata brief identifies the spaces a contractor may need to inspect and the person who can arrange legitimate access. List questions about the suite, common spaces and meter location without assuming that any of them can be opened on the day. If an interruption might affect other people, ask the building representative and contractor how the need would be assessed and coordinated. Do not arrange an informal shutoff yourself or promise that a visit will not affect another suite.

Keep an assessment appointment distinct from permission to carry out installation work. A first visit may establish missing information or identify a different scope. Ask what can be determined from the supplied documents, what requires site observation and what remains conditional on building or utility records. This creates a practical next step even when the initial answer is incomplete. It also prevents an owner from ordering an appliance on the mistaken assumption that an appointment confirmation was an acceptance of the installation proposal.

sections.heading: Check the responsible permit authority before work begins
paragraphs: Vancouver’s gas-permit page says new natural-gas installations and alterations require a permit. It describes City jurisdiction using building type, meter pressure and connected load, and directs other installations to Technical Safety BC. The City also says strata owners cannot use its homeowner gas-permit exception and must hire a licensed contractor. Have the contractor confirm the authority and permit path for the actual proposal; “Vancouver address” alone does not settle every jurisdictional boundary.

Technical Safety BC’s alteration bulletin explains that additions, replacements and removals are alterations requiring the appropriate permit before work begins. A replacement therefore should not be assumed exempt simply because there was already a gas appliance in that space. Ask the quotation to identify permit responsibility and the records expected at completion. Keep property approval, regulatory permission and technical assessment as separate items in your checklist. This guide is not an interpretation of a particular strata agreement, a permit application or a declaration that the proposed work complies with the applicable requirements.

sections.heading: Pressure and meter records need professional interpretation
paragraphs: An existing meter is a starting point for identification, not a promise of spare capacity. Give the contractor documented meter information and the current and proposed equipment list. If utility involvement is needed, FortisBC provides a gas-service upgrade process. Ask who will communicate with the utility and what information they require. Do not submit a request describing an unverified increase as established fact, and do not assume that a service upgrade is either necessary or unnecessary before the professional assessment.

Pressure figures are meaningful only with the correct unit and context. Distinguish a value copied from a document from a field measurement performed by a qualified person. The planner accepts records; it does not instruct homeowners to test pressure, alter regulators or convert a meter’s flow rating into approved appliance capacity. Keep questions about supply pressure, allowable pressure drop, fittings and mixed materials on the contractor’s assessment list. An attractive diagram and a precise-looking subtotal do not reduce those technical questions to a yes-or-no software result.

sections.heading: Compare complete proposals and keep the handover usable
paragraphs: Request a written proposal that names the actual appliance and distinguishes assessment, disconnection, installation, electrical coordination, permits and commissioning. Ask who handles any cabinet changes, restoration, removal and return visits. An allowance for unseen work should state how the uncertainty will be resolved and how a change is approved. Compare proposals against the same project brief; otherwise a lower headline price may simply describe less work. This guide establishes no installed price, appointment, stock position or rebate eligibility.

At handover, retain the supplied appliance identification, applicable manuals, completed work record and any relevant permit or declaration information. Ask the contractor to explain which owner instructions apply and which future questions need qualified service. If the final route or equipment differs from the initial sketch, update your records and keep the earlier version identified as preliminary. A later contractor should be able to tell what was proposed, what was actually supplied and which information remains unknown. That is the useful outcome of the planning exercise: a traceable brief and an assessed decision, rather than a drawing mistaken for permission.

faqs.question: Can a stove gas line solve a full electrical panel?
faqs.answer: It may be worth assessing, but it is not a guaranteed solution. A gas stove still needs the electrical supply specified for its exact model. Have a qualified electrician assess the panel and circuit, and a licensed gas contractor assess the proposed gas line, shared loads and approvals.

faqs.question: Can a Fairview strata owner install the gas range under a homeowner permit?
faqs.answer: The City of Vancouver says strata owners cannot use its homeowner gas-permit exception and must hire a licensed contractor. Confirm the responsible authority and the actual project scope with that contractor.

faqs.question: Does the 35-foot example tell me which pipe size to use?
faqs.answer: No. It only sums the hypothetical entered route:18+12+5 feet. Gas type, pressure arrangement, materials, fittings, connected loads and the applicable sizing method require qualified assessment.

faqs.question: Should I enter 18,000 BTU/h for the Frigidaire GCFG3060BF?
faqs.answer: Not as a complete appliance input merely because 18,000 appears beside a component in the Canadian specification. Obtain the actual complete input and fuel configuration from the rating information and qualified review; otherwise leave the proposed load unknown.

faqs.question: Does strata approval establish available meter capacity?
faqs.answer: No. Property permission and technical supply assessment are separate decisions. Keep their evidence separate and ask the contractor whether utility confirmation is needed.

faqs.question: Is the featured kitchen a Fairview customer installation?
faqs.answer: No. It is the official Frigidaire product photograph, credited to the manufacturer and used as a model illustration. No customer location, partnership, endorsement or completed installation is claimed.

title: Adding a gas barbecue in Vancouver: when the fitter needs a meter exchange
description: What FortisBC asks for when a gas fitter identifies a service upgrade, and which details to collect before the call.
intro: A new barbecue on a quotation raises two separate questions: what the appliance needs, and whether the existing gas service can supply the property after the addition. The homeowner can help assemble the equipment list. The gas fitter determines what to request from the utility.

sections.heading: Get the two figures from your fitter
paragraphs: FortisBC’s service-upgrade instructions ask for the required delivery pressure and the total load in BTU, along with the fitter’s name and telephone number. A number from the barbecue listing describes one appliance. Passing that number to the utility as the whole property load can send the enquiry back to the contractor for clarification.

sections.heading: Make one handoff before setting an installation date
paragraphs: Ask your fitter to put the requested service details and a callback number together on the estimate. If a meter exchange is needed, use FortisBC’s Construction Services contact on its upgrade page. Keep the utility reference with the installer’s quotation so both parties can identify the same request before you book the work.

faqs.question: Does every barbecue addition need a larger meter?
faqs.answer: FortisBC describes an exchange when the fitter determines that the increased use calls for a different regulator or larger meter. Ask your fitter about your actual equipment.

intro: You may be able to add a natural gas barbecue at a Grandview-Woodland property, but the distance to the patio does not decide the answer. Start with the exact natural gas appliance, a sketch of the known supply route, the longest measured route and the other connected appliances. Then have a qualified gas contractor assess the supply, location, installation and permit scope. Use the Gasfitter.ca sketch planner to build that brief before requesting an assessment; its totals organize your inputs and do not approve pipe size, pressure drop or meter capacity.

This guide works through a barbecue-specific planning exercise rather than assuming every Vancouver backyard has the same system. The example appliance is the Weber Spirit E-325 Natural Gas, Canadian part number 1500844. The manufacturer’s current Canadian product page identifies that fuel version and lists 31,000 BTU per hour for its main burners. Confirm the actual appliance’s rating plate and matching documents before using any figure in a real project. The worked distances below are invented teaching inputs, never measurements from a customer installation.

sections.heading: Start with your property, rather than a neighbourhood assumption
paragraphs: The City identifies Grandview-Woodland as a Vancouver neighbourhood associated with Commercial Drive and extending south toward Trout Lake. That local context helps identify the project area; it cannot reveal your meter pressure, concealed piping or permission to alter shared property. A useful enquiry starts with the actual property arrangement: detached home, rented premises or a strata property, along with who can authorize changes. Do not infer a building’s gas capacity from its street, apparent age or a nearby installation.

Describe the outdoor space you actually want to use. A freestanding barbecue beside an open patio is a different proposal from a built-in counter, covered area or balcony. Take ordinary photographs of the intended position and surrounding features when it is safe to do so. Show access routes, doors and nearby equipment without asserting that any separation is compliant. A contractor needs enough context to identify questions; a polished photograph with important surroundings cropped out is a poor substitute for a clear brief.

Separate your preferred cooking position from the proposed gas outlet. Those are related decisions, but they are not necessarily the same point on the sketch. Record where you want to stand, where people normally walk and where the barbecue would be stored. Ask the assessor to confirm an acceptable equipment and connection arrangement. Do not make a hose reach a preferred position by improvising extensions or routing it through a walking path. An initial drawing should expose a difficult layout before patio work or appliance purchasing makes it expensive to change.

sections.heading: Identify the natural gas model before entering its input
paragraphs: For this exercise, write “Weber Spirit E-325 Natural Gas, 1500844” in the appliance notes. Keep the manufacturer’s Canadian product link with that entry. The value 31,000 BTU per hour comes from that page’s main-burner input specification; it is an equipment record for this example, not an allowance granted by the existing house piping. If the appliance label or supplied documentation differs, stop using the example value and ask the supplier or contractor to reconcile the exact version.

A propane version with a similar name is a different fuel appliance. Weber’s natural gas owner’s manual warns against attempting to use one fuel in the other version and against modifying the appliance. Its manual also covers several Spirit variants, so retain the exact model and the manual revision together. A family name on a search result does not establish that every instruction or feature applies to your unit. Download the matching documents from the manufacturer and keep the rating information available for the professional assessment.

The supplied photograph is an official Weber cooking-surface detail associated with the E-325 natural gas product page. It illustrates the barbecue subject; it is not evidence of a Vancouver installation, a connection arrangement or a performance test carried out by Gasfitter.ca. Product imagery can make the project easier to understand, while the model records supply the actual technical starting point. Neither should be used to imply that the photographed scene demonstrates all clearances, local permissions or installation requirements at your property.

sections.heading: Make the longest measured route visible in the planner
paragraphs: Open the gas-line sketch planner and create a project with British Columbia and natural gas selected. Add the existing supply point and known junctions, then add a BBQ appliance for the proposed addition. Use the available node controls to position the appliance and draw connections representing the known arrangement. The useful result is a readable project sketch that distinguishes existing information from proposed work. It is not a construction drawing or a direction to connect the appliance yourself.

Use measured route lengths from reliable existing records or safely accessible observations. A straight line across a plan is not automatically the route the gas follows. Include changes of direction and vertical travel in the information you provide, and identify concealed sections as unknown. The planner has a section-length entry and a separate vertical-distance entry: add vertical distance separately only when it has not already been included in the measured section. Otherwise the same travel can be counted twice and make the sketch misleading.

Consider a fictional arrangement with a 20-foot supply-to-junction section, a 15-foot junction-to-existing-appliance section and a 25-foot proposed barbecue section from that junction. The two entered routes are 35 feet and 45 feet. The longest entered route is therefore 45 feet, even though the new barbecue branch itself is only 25 feet. These are simple distance sums used to explain the drawing. They do not select a pipe diameter or show that any existing pipe can carry the added load.

Now suppose the proposed barbecue route includes a separate 5-foot rise not already counted in its 25 feet. Entering that additional travel makes its recorded route 50 feet. If the 25-foot measurement already followed the whole route including the rise, leave the extra field empty or zero and explain what the measurement covers. Save a note identifying the source of each measurement. A contractor can then challenge one uncertain section without having to discard an otherwise useful drawing or guess how the total was assembled.

sections.heading: A long route and a high shared load answer different questions
paragraphs: A longest-run approach considers the route through the relevant system or pressure section alongside the load carried by individual sections. Énergir’s technical explanation describes surveying appliances and distances, identifying pressure arrangements and regulators, and considering branch loads. It also identifies material, available pressure and routing as sizing inputs. This explains why a single distance cannot settle the barbecue question. Its technical overview is background reading, not a substitute for the applicable British Columbia requirements and a site-specific design.

On the fictional sketch, the shared 20-foot section serves more than the barbecue. Its assessment depends on the appliances downstream, rather than the new barbecue input alone. Enter known existing appliance inputs from appropriate records, and keep unknown values visibly unknown. The planner can total the values supplied to it, but a partial equipment list creates a partial total. Calling that number “the house load” would conceal missing information and could lead someone to misunderstand what still needs assessment.

Do not add a speculative furnace, pool heater or future outdoor kitchen as though it is already installed. Identify proposed future equipment separately and ask whether the contractor should assess that scenario now. A useful comparison states what changes between the current and proposed layouts. For example, the barbecue-only proposal and a later barbecue-plus-heater proposal should have distinct notes and version names. That makes the assessment request clear without turning an unselected future appliance into a fictitious confirmed load.

sections.heading: Record pressure, material and meter information honestly
paragraphs: The planner can retain supply-pressure information and its unit, along with meter-rating details where those records are available. Record the provenance and context: an existing contractor document, an applicable utility response or an appliance record. Leave unfamiliar or uncertain information blank and ask for confirmation. A pressure value without a unit is ambiguous, and a meter label is not a certificate that a particular amount of capacity is available for an addition. The planner does not make that determination.

Where known, identify the piping material and any documented changes of material or regulators in the project notes. Do not open a wall, dig near services, disconnect equipment or adjust a regulator to complete a web form. A preliminary record can say that a section is concealed and requires professional verification. That is a useful finding because it identifies the next assessment task. Guessing a material to make every field look complete removes the very uncertainty the visit needs to resolve.

Technical Safety BC’s pressure-drop bulletin explains that inadequate supply can affect other connected appliances and that applicable code requirements cannot simply be replaced by an appliance’s apparent ability to operate. FortisBC’s connection guidance also directs customers to their gas fitter for the delivery pressure needed for the intended appliances and piping. Ask the contractor to identify the required supply conditions and any utility coordination. Do not treat turning on a barbecue as a household capacity test or attempt to create a low-pressure condition yourself.

sections.heading: Check the actual outdoor and permit scope
paragraphs: The Weber manual identifies this as an outdoor appliance and warns against built-in or slide-in installation for the models it covers. Bring the complete matching instructions to the discussion, including location and surrounding-construction questions. Do not use a general patio photograph to approve a covered or partly enclosed position. This guide deliberately does not provide a universal setback diagram: the actual model instructions, site arrangement and applicable authority need to be considered together before a location is accepted.

Vancouver’s gas-permit page states that new natural gas installations and alterations require a permit, and it describes the installations administered by the City versus other installations directed to Technical Safety BC. Ask the contractor to confirm the correct authority for the actual property and system. Neighbourhood identity does not determine that boundary. Keep the permit responsibility explicit in the proposed scope, rather than assuming a new outlet is an incidental task outside the main installation assessment.

Property authorization is a separate question from gas permitting. If you rent, or the work affects shared property, establish who must approve the proposed alteration before asking anyone to proceed. Keep that answer with the project brief. A supplier confirming the barbecue’s model is not approving work on the building. Similarly, a property manager allowing an assessment does not establish that the gas supply is suitable. Separating these decisions makes a quote easier to compare and prevents an early conversation from being mistaken for a complete go-ahead.

sections.heading: Turn the sketch into an assessment request
paragraphs: Export the planner’s project record and a readable summary, retaining a dated copy for yourself. Describe the request in plain language: you want an assessment of adding the specified natural gas barbecue at the marked outdoor location. List the documents supplied, the known route measurements, the largest entered route and the uncertainties. Ask what additional information or site access the assessor needs. Include only relevant project details and use the appropriate private enquiry channel for address and contact information.

Ask the proposal to distinguish assessment, installation work, any supply changes, permit handling and handover. Clarify whether patio reinstatement, access work and coordination with other trades are included. These are scope questions rather than requests for a guaranteed price from a web drawing. If a quote assumes a route or existing capacity, ask how and when those assumptions will be verified. Compare proposals on a common documented scenario so that a smaller scope is not mistaken for an equivalent cheaper installation.

After assessment, update your saved project with confirmed findings and keep them separate from the original assumptions. If the barbecue location or model changes, send the revised version before work proceeds and ask whether the assessment remains applicable. Keep the final installation documents, appliance manual and any applicable permit or inspection records together. The planner’s practical benefit is continuity: you can explain what was proposed, what was unknown and what changed, while the qualified professionals retain responsibility for design, installation and required verification.

faqs.question: Does a 50-foot longest run mean I can install the barbecue?
faqs.answer: No. That distance is only one input. The qualified assessor must consider the actual route, section loads, material, pressure arrangement, appliance requirements, existing system and applicable rules. Gasfitter.ca’s planner records and summarizes your information without approving pipe size or supply capacity.

faqs.question: What barbecue input should I use for the example?
faqs.answer: Weber’s Canadian page for Spirit E-325 Natural Gas part 1500844 lists 31,000 BTU per hour for the main burners. Treat that as this example’s source record. Verify the actual appliance label and matching documentation before using it for a real assessment; do not copy the value to a different model.

faqs.question: Can I use a propane E-325 with a natural gas outlet?
faqs.answer: Do not assume that matching family names mean matching fuels. Weber warns against attempted use of the wrong fuel and modification. Confirm the exact natural gas model and supplied instructions with the manufacturer or supplier, and have the installation assessed by a qualified gas contractor.

faqs.question: Should I measure a hidden gas route myself?
faqs.answer: Do not expose concealed or buried services to complete the planner. Use suitable existing records and safely accessible observations, mark unknown sections clearly and ask the contractor what needs professional verification. A partial honest sketch is more useful than an apparently complete route based on guesses.

faqs.question: What should I send with a Grandview-Woodland enquiry?
faqs.answer: Send the selected model and fuel documents, a dated planner export, safely obtained location photographs, the source of known measurements and a list of unresolved questions. State the property arrangement and authorization status. Ask for the assessment, permit and installation scope without describing the sketch as an approval.

intro: Before moving a gas stove during a Mount Pleasant kitchen renovation, agree on the proposed appliance and location, identify the gas work that may change, and coordinate that assessment with the kitchen designer and other responsible trades. A cabinet drawing or an existing gas connection does not establish that the new arrangement is suitable. Check the City of Vancouver’s current renovation and gas-permit guidance, then ask the qualified contractor to define the actual scope before demolition, ordering or finishing decisions make changes harder.

This guide follows the project from the first layout discussion to handover. Its purpose is to help you give each person the same reliable information: what exists, what is proposed, which decisions remain open and who will confirm them. It does not provide disconnection, reconnection or pipe-sizing instructions. The featured photograph is GE Appliances’ archival Café kitchen-suite press photograph from the 2019 KBIS collection. It illustrates a cooking-appliance setting, not a Mount Pleasant property or a project undertaken by Gasfitter.ca.

sections.heading: Decide whether the project is a replacement, a move or both
paragraphs: Begin with the change itself rather than the shopping list. Replacing a stove in its existing position, moving the current stove to another wall and installing a different appliance in a revised kitchen are three different proposals. A combined project can include both relocation and equipment changes. Write down the existing appliance, the proposed appliance and the intended location separately. If you are still comparing layouts, present them as options rather than giving different trades conflicting versions of a supposedly settled plan.

An original example makes the distinction clear. One brief might say, “We want to replace the existing range in the same cabinet opening and need the proposed model assessed.” Another might say, “We want the cooking area on the opposite wall and need the layout reviewed before cabinets are ordered.” These are planning examples, not reported local jobs. The second introduces route and coordination questions even if the appliance itself stays the same. The first can still raise compatibility and surrounding-installation questions; unchanged location is not the same as unchanged scope.

sections.heading: Confirm the property arrangement and project decision-maker
paragraphs: Identify who owns or manages the property and who can approve the work. For a strata unit, rented home or property with several responsible parties, distinguish the person using the kitchen from the person authorizing alterations. Ask which property documents or permissions the designer and contractor need to see. Keep those arrangements separate from municipal approvals and technical assessment. An appliance purchase, a contractor enquiry and an accepted renovation scope are different stages, and none should be quietly substituted for another in the project folder.

Mount Pleasant is a neighbourhood within Vancouver, as described by the City’s area page. That geographic context is useful for identifying the project location, but it does not establish your building’s age, layout, piping or approval history. Describe the actual property and any existing documents you have. Do not assume that a guide written for the neighbourhood represents every kitchen there. If responsibility for shared equipment, access or a proposed alteration is unclear, make that a question to resolve before asking a trade to proceed on an assumed authorization.

sections.heading: Give the designer and gas contractor the same appliance record
paragraphs: Collect the proposed appliance’s manufacturer, model designation, fuel version and applicable installation documentation. Keep the supplier’s quotation with the identifying record, but do not assume a short sales description includes every installation detail. If the equipment has not been selected, mark the model as undecided and ask when selection must be finalized. A kitchen plan based on an approximate appliance opening can become inconsistent with the actual equipment if the model changes while cabinets, surfaces or related work are already being ordered.

For existing equipment, retain the records already available, such as a manual, invoice or safely visible identifying information. Do not move a connected stove or remove components to create a more complete enquiry. Label old and proposed documents clearly so nobody uses the former appliance’s information as if it described the replacement. The historic Café photograph accompanying this article is not a specification source for your project. It does not establish an exact model, current availability, required clearances or suitability for a Canadian installation.

sections.heading: Distinguish room measurements from gas-route measurements
paragraphs: A kitchen drawing and a gas-route sketch answer different questions. The room drawing can identify the intended appliance position, adjacent cabinets, other equipment and the proposed work area. The gas sketch can organize known or proposed upstream connections and measured route sections. Do not treat a dimension between two cabinet faces as the assessed gas-route length. Explain what each measurement represents and who supplied it. Where a route is concealed or uncertain, the drawing should show a missing fact rather than disguising it with a neat line.

Gasfitter.ca’s planner adds the section lengths entered along each connected appliance path. Its drawing is not to scale, and moving a symbol across the screen does not change the entered distance. Additional vertical distance should be entered separately only when it is not already part of the section measurement. The tool does not calculate an approved fitting allowance or select a pipe diameter. Use it to preserve the information you have and to identify the questions the contractor needs to answer, not to turn an early cabinet layout into an installation design.

sections.heading: Ask what happens before demolition starts
paragraphs: Agree when the existing cooking appliance needs to be taken out of use and who will handle the relevant gas work. The general renovation schedule should identify that step before other trades begin removing cabinets or working around the equipment. A demolition crew should not have to infer that the stove has been dealt with because it appears on an empty-room drawing. Ask the responsible contractor how the work will be coordinated and what confirmation the project lead needs before the next stage begins.

Do not disconnect equipment, disturb a live connection or move the stove as a shortcut to help the renovation begin. The planning task is to assign responsibility and make the sequence visible. Ask what temporary arrangements are needed for the household and which parts of the kitchen will be unavailable. Keep the timing realistic by distinguishing a requested date from a confirmed appointment. If another part of the project is delayed, tell the affected trades promptly rather than letting an old schedule operate as an instruction after the circumstances have changed.

sections.heading: Coordinate ventilation, electrical work and surrounding finishes
paragraphs: Moving the cooking area can affect more than the gas connection. Ask the designer and the appropriate trades which associated ventilation, electrical and surrounding-installation questions need assessment. Record who is responsible for each part and which model documents they are using. Do not infer that an existing hood, outlet or cabinet arrangement will suit the revised location simply because it served the old stove. A photograph of an attractive showroom kitchen is useful for discussing appearance, but it is not evidence that the same arrangement is appropriate at your property.

Keep the scope questions connected without confusing responsibility. The gas contractor should not be expected to approve an unrelated trade’s work through a general comment on the kitchen drawing. Similarly, a cabinetry decision should not silently determine where regulated work must go without the relevant assessment. Ask for the decisions that need to be confirmed before a cabinet or countertop order is released. Where a point remains open, label it as a dependency rather than relying on several separate emails to preserve the uncertainty.

sections.heading: Include the connected system when discussing a different stove
paragraphs: If the proposed appliance changes the gas demand under consideration, provide its actual input information from the applicable record. The planner’s input field is in BTU per hour. Do not substitute oven volume, electrical demand, a heating-output figure or the value listed for another appliance. Where the input remains unknown, leave it unknown. A plausible-looking number can make an incomplete proposal appear settled and can be copied into later documents without anybody noticing that the original assumption was never confirmed.

Also identify the other relevant appliances on the supply being assessed, while distinguishing confirmed connections from questions. A stove relocation is not automatically a review of the whole property, so ask what the proposed assessment includes. Pressure and meter-rating fields in the planner retain entered records; they do not approve pressure loss, choose material-specific tables or certify spare capacity. Ask who will confirm the supply arrangement and whether another responsible party needs to be involved. Keep that finding separate from your preliminary drawing and the initial equipment inventory.

sections.heading: Check the City of Vancouver renovation and gas-permit guidance
paragraphs: The City’s current home-renovation page distinguishes cosmetic changes from work such as moving existing gas lines and other services. Read it alongside the gas-permit page rather than treating a kitchen project as one generic permission question. Describe the actual proposal when asking the City or contractor what applies. A cabinet replacement, an appliance move and an alteration to regulated systems may raise different issues within the same renovation. The purpose of checking early is to identify those issues before the scope is obscured by a single label such as “kitchen refresh.”

The gas-permit guidance also explains the installations administered by Vancouver and circumstances involving Technical Safety BC. Have the responsible professional identify the authority and process for the actual work. This article does not determine applicant eligibility, promise a permit outcome or certify a proposed layout. When the scope is agreed, record who will obtain the required permits and provide the relevant completion information. Keep the current official links in the project folder so a later change can be checked against the real requirements rather than against an earlier informal assumption.

sections.heading: Build one change record for equipment and layout revisions
paragraphs: Kitchen plans often pass through several versions. Give each accepted drawing a date or version and identify which appliance record belongs with it. If you change the proposed stove or move the cooking position again, tell the people assessing the work and ask whether their earlier assumptions remain valid. Do not rely on a revised image in a messaging thread to notify every trade. The project lead should be able to point to one current brief and explain which earlier version it replaces.

A useful change record states what changed, why it changed, who needs to review it and whether price or timing remains open. For example, a different appliance choice might require a new review before an existing quote can be treated as applicable. That is not proof that additional work will necessarily be needed; it is a reason to confirm rather than guess. Keep an unaccepted proposal separate from an authorized change. This makes later comparisons and handover questions easier to resolve without reconstructing the project from memory.

sections.heading: Compare quotations by responsibilities and exclusions
paragraphs: Ask each business what its proposal covers. Does it include assessing the intended location, the relevant existing arrangement, the proposed appliance documents and the work that follows? Which questions are left to a site visit or another trade? Who handles finishing, access, return visits and revisions? A quotation for a narrow connection task should not be compared as if it necessarily covers a broader relocation and renovation review. Request enough detail to understand the work represented by the price instead of assuming that similar totals describe equivalent services.

Keep those responsibilities visible in the overall renovation agreement. If the designer, general contractor, gas contractor and appliance supplier each have a different role, identify where information passes between them. Confirm which business accepts the work and the basis on which an appointment becomes confirmed. Gasfitter.ca publishes planning information; an article or email enquiry does not create a booking or establish local availability. Choose the professional arrangement directly and retain the accepted scope, questions and exclusions with the appliance and layout records.

sections.heading: Prepare for the stage before finishes hide the work
paragraphs: Ask the responsible contractor and project lead which checks or records are needed before work becomes inaccessible behind completed finishes. Do not decide on behalf of an authority that a site visit or document is unnecessary because the work looks simple. Equally, do not call work “inspected” unless the actual record supports that description. Agree on the next-stage requirements and who will communicate completion so the people installing finishes are working from confirmed project information rather than a presumed green light.

This coordination is especially useful when separate trades return at different times. A person arriving to finish cabinets or surfaces should know which work is ready for the next stage and which part remains outstanding. Keep the communication factual: what was completed, what was checked, what document is available and what still needs to happen. A photograph can support the record but does not replace the responsible person’s confirmation. If a discrepancy appears between the current drawing and the actual work, raise it before treating the drawing as an accurate handover record.

sections.heading: Keep the handover useful for the next owner or service visit
paragraphs: At completion, gather the documents supplied for the actual equipment and work: the applicable appliance information, accepted changes, relevant permit or completion records, and the contractor’s service or warranty details. Ask who to contact if a question concerns the appliance rather than the renovation work. Keep unresolved items clearly identified. A paid invoice, a product registration and a regulatory record establish different things, so store them with understandable descriptions instead of interpreting any one document as proof of every aspect of the project.

Save the final accepted layout with the equipment record and keep earlier versions distinguishable. If another appliance change is proposed later, the next person should be able to identify what was actually installed without relying on a showroom photograph or an old shopping list. The most useful outcome of preparation is a traceable sequence: initial proposal, professional assessment, accepted scope, recorded changes and completed work. That sequence helps a later enquiry begin with reliable information and reduces the chance that a preliminary planning assumption survives as an alleged installation fact.

faqs.question: Can I move a connected gas stove myself to begin demolition?
faqs.answer: Do not move or disconnect it as a renovation shortcut. Arrange the relevant gas work with the qualified professional and coordinate its timing before other trades begin. Ask what confirmation the project lead needs before the next stage proceeds.

faqs.question: Does moving the same stove mean the supply assessment stays unchanged?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. A different position may change the route and the surrounding project scope even when the appliance is retained. Describe the actual change and ask the contractor which existing assumptions remain applicable instead of treating unchanged equipment as an unchanged installation.

faqs.question: Does a cabinet drawing establish the correct gas-line length?
faqs.answer: No. Room dimensions and gas-route measurements are different information. The planner adds entered route sections but does not survey concealed piping, calculate an approved pressure drop or select a pipe size. Leave unknown route details visible for assessment.

faqs.question: Is the featured kitchen a Mount Pleasant renovation?
faqs.answer: No. It is GE Appliances’ official 2019 KBIS Café Matte White Kitchen Suite press photograph, cropped and branded for this guide. It is not a customer project, a current product recommendation or evidence of a particular Canadian installation.

faqs.question: What should I send before asking for a stove-relocation quote?
faqs.answer: Describe the property arrangement, existing and proposed appliance, intended location and renovation stage. Include the applicable model documents and current layout if available, identify unknowns and ask what assessment is needed. Keep credentials, access codes and unrelated private records out of the general enquiry.
